extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, historians, and policymakers interested in 19th-century American Indian policy
extracted.subtask_short: future condition of Native American tribes
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic chapter discussing the likely destiny of Native American nations under pressure from European/American expansion, including social, economic, and political causes that affect their capacity to 'civilize' or survive. Focuses on institutional, cultural, and policy factors that determine outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two alternatives: war or civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indians had only the two alternatives of war or civilization; in other words, they must either have destroyed the Europeans or become their equals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an overarching binary determining the fate of Indian nations—either successfully resist European encroachment militarily, or assimilate to European levels of social organization and power. The text implies both options are now practically impossible for most tribes given resource disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilization requires fixation and agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to succeed in civilizing a people, it is first necessary to fix it; which cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil; the Indians ought in the first place to have been accustomed to agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues civilization is a long social process transmitted across generations in a stable location; attempts to teach knowledge without removing nomadism (wandering propensities) fail. Examples: Jesuits in Canada and Puritans in New England—'civilization began in the cabin, but it soon retired to expire in the woods.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunter lifestyle resists civilization more than pastoralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all nations, those submit to civilization with the most difficulty which habitually live by the chase. Pastoral tribes often change place of abode but follow regular migrations; hunters' dwellings vary with the animals they pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the erratic, mobile nature of hunting societies, the continuity and accumulation of social knowledge needed for civilization are undermined. Attempts to civilize without addressing mobility are doomed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride and contempt of labor obstruct adoption of agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: They consider labor not merely as an evil, but as a disgrace; so that their pride prevents them from becoming civilized, as much as their indolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural valuation of hunting, war, and valor places manual agriculture and sedentary labor beneath social standing; elder warriors mock those who use the hoe. This psychological/social barrier is as significant as practical obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilization is cumulative and generational
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilization is the result of a long social process which takes place in the same spot, and is handed down from one generation to another, each one profiting by the experience of the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term or piecemeal interventions (schools, missions) without stable settlement and intergenerational transmission will not create lasting civilization. The text contrasts how conquered barbarians who command physical force can adopt and then transmit civilized knowledge, whereas conquered peoples who are also intellectually inferior cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful acculturation occurs when barbarians are conquerors, not the conquered
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever they derive knowledge from a foreign people, they stood towards it in the relation of conquerors, and not of a conquered nation... But when the side on which the physical force lies, also possesses an intellectual preponderance, the conquered party seldom [becomes] civilized; it retreats, or is destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical pattern: when barbarians bring force and then receive knowledge, they can become civilized over time; when a people are both militarily and intellectually dominated, assimilation fails and decline follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact with Europeans when semi-barbarous tends to oppression and destitution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the misfortune of Indians to be brought into contact with a civilized people, which is also... the most avaricious nation on the globe, whilst they are still semi-barbarian: to find despots in their instructors, and to receive knowledge from the hand of oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nature of the European contact matters: if the dominating society is avaricious and oppressive, the transfer of knowledge/civilization is corrupted by exploitation. Examples include loss of land, forced labor, and social demotion when Indians attempt to adopt European life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic competition with Europeans undermines Indian agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Indians undertake to imitate their European neighbors, and to till the earth like the settlers, they are immediately exposed to a very formidable competition... The European is skilled... the Indian is a rough beginner... the former reaps abundant crops without difficulty, the latter meets with a thousand obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if Indians adopt agriculture, they lack market access, capital, experience, and community support; white settlers' superior skills and markets force Indians out economically, causing ruin or abandonment of farming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relocation (removal) is insecure and only delays dispossession
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States pledge themselves to the observance of the obligation; but the territory which they at present occupy was formerly secured to them by the most solemn oaths of Anglo-American faith... In a few years the same white population which now flocks around them, will track them to the solitudes of the Arkansas; they will then be exposed to the same evils without the same remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government promises to provide a permanent refuge (e.g., beyond the Mississippi/Arkansas) are unreliable because settler pressure and incursions recur; relocation merely postpones the same pattern of encroachment and eventual loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-level tyranny forces removal; federal inability facilitates expulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyrannical measures which have been adopted by the legislatures of the Southern States... If we consider... we shall be convinced that the entire expulsion of the Indians is the final result to which the efforts of their policy are directed... The federal government, which is not able to protect the Indians, would fain mitigate the hardships of their lot; and, with this intention, proposals have been made to transport them into more remote regions at the public cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict between state hostility and federal promises produces a dynamic where states push Indians out and the federal government offers removal as a mitigation—both together result in effective dispossession and expulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties and solemn guarantees often fail in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifth article of the treaty made with the Creeks... 'The United States solemnly guarantee to the Creek nation all their land within the limits of the United States.'... The Union treats the Indians with less cupidity and rigor than the policy of the several States, but the two governments are alike destitute of good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal or treaty guarantees are cited but the author highlights recurring violations and the practical ineffectiveness of such guarantees in preventing encroachment and dispossession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-race populations accelerate acculturation
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of European habits has been remarkably accelerated among these Indians by the mixed race which has sprung up... the half-blood forms the natural link between civilization and barbarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermarriage and mixed families are portrayed as vectors that transmit 'intelligence' and habits of civilization into native communities, facilitating cultural change where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional cases (Cherokees) show capacity but not general success
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cherokees went further; they created a written language; established a permanent form of government... The success of the Cherokees proves that the Indians are capable of civilization, but it does not prove that they will succeed in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples where Indians adopted institutions of 'civilization' (written language, government, newspapers) demonstrate capability, but structural pressures (competition, state hostility, federal unreliability) make general success unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural attachment to freedom and wilderness resists settled life
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in the adventurous life of the hunter a certain irresistible charm... he contrasts the independence which he possessed amongst his equals with the servile position which he occupies in civilized society... The whites offer him a sum... he quits the plough, resumes his native arms, and returns to the wilderness forever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological/political attachment to autonomy, adventure, and the social esteem accorded to hunting/war leads many who try sedentary agriculture to abandon it and return to wilderness life, undermining long-term settlement efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall determinism: extinction or assimilation into European society
rubrics_metrics.description: From whichever side we consider the destinies of the aborigines of North America, their calamities appear to be irremediable: if they continue barbarous, they are forced to retire; if they attempt to civilize their manners, the contact of a more civilized community subjects them to oppression and destitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author concludes a near-inevitable trajectory: continued marginalization and decline, whether through forced removal, economic ruin upon attempted acculturation, or gradual extinction—policy choices and cultural traits combine to make redress unlikely.
